To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rate of hydroxylation of phenylalanin is sigmoidal with respect to substrate concentration and that glucagon increases the activity of the phenylalanine dehydrogenase only at low, near physiological, phenylalanine concentrations.

the rate of phenylalanin metabolism in isolated rat hepatocytes is controlled by the availability of phenylalan, that glucagon increases phenylalanin hydroxylase (PAH) activity in isolated hepatocytes, and that diabetes increases phenylalan in metabolism in isolated hepatocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the control of phenylketonuria, a disease caused by a defect in phenylalanine metabolism.
the control of phenylalaine metabolism in the intact liver cell.
the regulation of phenylalaninemia, and in particular the role of glucagon.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glucagon does not affect the hydroxylase reaction in vivo.
glucagon stimulates phenylalanine oxidation in vivo, and that this effect is enhanced in diabetes.
the rate of phenylalaninolysis is controlled by the rate of formation and/or availability of phenylalaninel-tyrosine aminotransferase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glucagon does not act by increasing the activity of phenylalanin hydroxylase but by increasing the flux through the hydroxylase.
the hydroxylase system is regulated by both substrate availability and by the action of the hormone glucagon.
phenylalanine metabolism is regulated in the liver cell by a number of factors, including the availability of phenylalanin...
The main takeaway from our work is that

glucagon does not affect the activity of the phenylalanine transaminase enzyme, and that the increase in phenylalanine flux seen in diabetes is due to a change in the enzyme's kinetic properties, rather than an increase in the enzyme's activity per se.
phenylalanine metabolism is controlled by the rate of formation and removal of phenylalaninemia.
the liver cell is a useful model system for the study of phenylalaninemia and its treatment.
